edition.title: Morning paper, Wednesday 7 October 2026

edition.intro: RBI decides on rates at 10 AM today, the insurance commission fight is getting louder, and two open-weight frontier models are due this month.

blocks.title: RBI decides today, and the street expects its first hike since February 2023

blocks.html: Economists expect the MPC under Governor Sanjay Malhotra to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points, from 5.25% to 5.50%. The rate has sat at 5.25% for nearly ten months after 125 bp of cuts in 2025. A hike is widely priced in. Less certain is whether the RBI also changes its stance. NDTV Profit lists rising inflation, higher crude, a weak rupee and a global shift to higher rates as the backdrop. Analysts quoted by BusinessLine say an in-line outcome could push the Nifty toward 23,000. That is their commentary, not a forecast of mine. The GST Council also meets today.
Why it matters to you: A hike moves your EMIs, bank margins and the rupee, which closed at 96.42 against the dollar, near its all-time low. Volatility around the 10 AM announcement is likely.
Source: NDTV Profit / Hindu BusinessLine, 6 Oct close

blocks.title: Insurers and brokers are fighting the IRDAI commission caps, and the decision window is now short

blocks.html: The Insurance Brokers Association of India told reporters on 6 October that it wants the 25 October deadline for feedback on IRDAI's paper "Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution" pushed to December. It wrote to the Finance Minister on 2 October and, per Reuters, to the Prime Minister. Its argument: the paper does not say how savings from lower distribution costs would reach policyholders, and IBAI estimates at least 10 lakh livelihoods could be at risk over five years. IBAI backs the ban on compulsory bundling of insurance with loans and tighter suitability rules.

The proposed caps, as Mint reports them: 2% to 5% for banks and lenders selling insurance with loans; 15% to 20% on health policies at purchase and 5% to 10% for renewals and portability; 5% to 10% on motor personal accident; 5% to 20% on first-year life commission depending on tenure. Moneycontrol reports that life insurers will push for targeted changes, not withdrawal, with credit-life and annuities the main flashpoints. IRDAI is said to have told the industry that a long delay or phased rollout could trigger front-loaded sales before the lower caps apply. CEO consultations are due this week, per the same report.

Why it matters to you: This is the economics Probus sits on. Comments close 25 October, and IRDAI is weighing 1 January or 1 April as the start date. Brokers are asking for more time. IRDAI reportedly does not want a long delay.
Source: CNBC-TV18 on IBAI / Moneycontrol on insurers / Mint, citing Reuters

blocks.title: Mistral and Reflection both announced frontier-class open-weight models, with weights due this month

blocks.html: Mistral Large 4 is in public preview from 6 October on Mistral Studio. It has 1 trillion parameters with 49 billion active, takes images and text, and was trained on 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own European datacenters. Weights are promised by the end of the month. Mistral says it is state of the art among open models on cybersecurity, finance and law, and competitive in coding. Those charts are Mistral's own.

Reflection, a Brooklyn startup, announced Beam on 5 October (US time): 501 billion parameters, 23 billion active per token, a one-million-token context and an Apache 2.0 licence when it ships "later this month". Reflection says Beam matches Z.ai's GLM 5.2 on hard reasoning tests with three to four times less compute, and trails Kimi K3. Quartz notes those claims are not independently verified. Beam is on a waitlist for now.

Why it matters to you: If both ship as promised, you get self-hostable models near the top of open-model benchmarks. That changes what a cost-sensitive prototype can run on. Treat the benchmarks as vendor claims until independent tests land.
Source: Mistral / The Decoder on Reflection / Quartz on Reflection

blocks.title: Nifty rebounded for a second day after an eight-week slide, with foreign money still leaving

blocks.html: The Nifty closed at 22,776.10 on Tuesday, up 0.98%, after an eight-week decline of 8.8%, its longest weekly losing run since 2020. FIIs sold ₹2,961 cr on 6 October and have been net sellers in all three October sessions, about ₹17,145 cr in total. DIIs bought ₹5,089 cr on the day and about ₹20,312 cr over the three sessions. Year to date on the same NSE series: FIIs net sold ₹4,20,212 cr, DIIs bought ₹6,59,847 cr. This series differs from the NSDL figures in yesterday's paper, so the totals do not match. Full recap is in Markets below.
Why it matters to you: The market is up on stock-specific Q2 buying, not a change in foreign flows. Domestic funds are absorbing the selling. RBI day will test that.
Source: Moneycontrol, NSE data / Hindu BusinessLine

blocks.title: Oolka is reportedly raising $45 M at roughly double its April valuation

blocks.html: Per four people cited by Moneycontrol, Bessemer would put in about $20 M and Prosus about $10 M, with about $15 M from existing backers Accel, Lightspeed and 8i Ventures. The valuation is around $200 M, up from about $90 M in April 2026. Oolka, founded in 2024 by former Meesho executive Utkrishta Kumar, says it is India's first agentic AI credit-management platform. Before this round it had raised about $21 M, per Tracxn. If it closes, it would be Prosus's fourth fintech bet in just over a month. Oolka, Bessemer and Prosus did not respond to Moneycontrol.

Why it matters to you: An AI credit-management app for consumers is drawing Bessemer and Prosus money. For an APM at an insurance aggregator, it is a read on how investors value agentic personal-finance products. It is a report of talks, not a closed round.
Source: Moneycontrol, 6 Oct

blocks.title: Melius raised $25 M after burning its first codebase

blocks.html: Three former Ramp engineers built an AI performance-marketing tool. After more than six months they decided it did not have legs, scrapped the codebase and rebuilt as an "agents lab for creative work", generating ad campaigns, images and video. Melius announced a $20 M Series A led by CRV and a $5 M seed led by General Catalyst. It claims more than $1 M in annualised revenue within two months of leaving stealth in July. Rivals include Higgsfield, valued at $5.4 B in August, which the co-founder says has passed $700 M in annualised revenue.
Why it matters to you: A founder pattern worth stealing, covered in the insight below.
Source: TechCrunch, 6 Oct

blocks.title: Set the kill criterion before you start

blocks.html: Melius did not rescue its first product. It decided it had not found the large market, cut it, and moved to an adjacent, bigger one.

For a side project, the cheap version is to write down in advance what traction by what date would make you stop. Decide the date and the number while you still feel neutral. That sentence is my reading of the Melius story, not something the founders said.

blocks.title: Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 is now the default Sonnet in the API, at unchanged prices

blocks.html: Per the Claude Code changelog as quoted by AI Coding Guide, Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) has a 1M context and costs $2 and $10 per million input and output tokens, with $0.20 cache reads. That is the same as Sonnet 5. I read the price from that secondary page, which says it matches Anthropic's pricing table. Anthropic also has a Sonnet 5.5 prompting page dated 6 October.
Why it matters to you: If your prototypes call Sonnet, they have moved to 5.5 with no price change.
Source: AI Coding Guide, quoting the Claude Code changelog / Anthropic docs, Sonnet 5.5 prompting

blocks.title: HeyGen's HyperFrames Studio: a free desktop video editor where your own coding agent does the work

blocks.html: It launched on Product Hunt on 5 October for Mac and Linux, marked free, and sign-in is a HeyGen account. Compositions are HTML with timing set by data attributes, and the Apache 2.0 renderer has no per-render fee. The agent is Claude Code or Codex on your machine, and runs bill to that account's plan or an API key. IndieFounder did not see a Windows build. The article is a third-party write-up, so I have not tested the app.
Why it matters to you: A video is a folder of HTML files, so you can version it and let Claude Code or Codex edit it. Worth a try if you make demo videos for side projects.
Source: IndieFounder

blocks.title: Claude Code 2.1.284 to 2.1.288: Sonnet 5.5 default, Claude Mods, new switches

blocks.html: Version 2.1.284 makes Sonnet 5.5 the default and adds /mcp reconnect all. 2.1.285 adds a switch to turn off WebFetch and a managed setting to limit which API providers a machine may use. 2.1.287 adds Claude Mods, which let plugins change deeper behaviour. This is from AI Coding Guide's summary of the changelog, not the changelog itself.
Why it matters to you: Worth updating for the new default. Mods are optional.
Source: AI Coding Guide, week of 4 Oct

blocks.title: Lovable swaps Visual edits for a preview toolbar

blocks.html: The changelog also adds line-level references in chat (for example Button.tsx:42) and a User insights profile for workspace admins. The changelog page does not show entry dates in what I read, so I cannot say when each shipped.
Why it matters to you: You can click an element, fix text inline, sketch on the preview or pin a comment, and queue the next change while Lovable is still working.

blocks.title: Give the model a sample and a reader, then delete the rules

blocks.html: Anthropic says it removed over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for its newest models with no measurable loss on its coding evaluations. It found it was over-constraining the model, and that its own instructions sometimes clashed, such as "leave documentation as appropriate" next to "DO NOT add comments". Its replacement instruction for code is one line: write code that reads like the surrounding code, matching comment density, naming and idiom.
That is guidance about code. The adaptation to writing is mine: replace a pile of style rules with a sample of your own writing and a named reader, and let the model match them.

Copy and pasteDraft a reply to the email below. The reader is [name, role] and they need to decide [what]. Write it so it reads like my two sample emails: match their sentence length, vocabulary and paragraph rhythm. Sample 1: [paste]. Sample 2: [paste]. Email to answer: [paste]. Do not add anything I did not give you.

If a draft still feels ornate, one extra tip is reported by AI Impactful, a third-party site, as an Anthropic suggestion for its model: "Please remove all mannered prose." I could not find that line on Anthropic's own pages, so treat it as unconfirmed, though it costs nothing to try. Sources: Anthropic, context engineering for Claude 5 models, 24 July and AI Impactful.

blocks.title: Essay: "If computers count all the petals, who tastes the cherries?"

blocks.html: Liam Spradlin, a designer, argues that tech culture holds a belief he calls computism: the idea that the world, humans included, is made of measurable bits that can be computed and governed by code. Read the full essay on Aeon (published 17 September, so older than this paper's news window, picked as a long read). I read all of it before writing the questions below. Read the essay first, then try them.

blocks.title: Reading comprehension

blocks.html: Q1. The author describes a chef who tried to brown lamb under a broiler the way "smacking it with a propane torch" would. The author uses this to show that:

items: (a) the chefs were poorly trained for the project
(b) the oven could not translate an embodied cooking instinct into anything its logic understood
(c) the oven needed a stronger broiler to match restaurant results
(d) home cooks are less skilled than professional chefs

blocks.html: Q2. According to the author, the "real tragedy" of computism is:

items: (a) that computers may become more intelligent than people
(b) that computers will take over some human activities
(c) that people might build a world where every petal is counted and lose the ability to taste the cherries
(d) that data collection will become too expensive to continue

blocks.html: Q3. Each of the following is used by the author as evidence or illustration EXCEPT:

items: (a) Google testing 41 shades of blue for its search links
(c) Descartes's picture of the body as a machine with a soul as its user
(d) a study showing that A/B testing lowered the revenue of most companies

blocks.title: Set: the pitch day

blocks.html: Six startups, A to F, pitch to one investor on one day, one after another, in six consecutive slots numbered 1 to 6. Each startup is in a different one of six sectors: Fintech, Health, Edtech, Agri, Logistics and Climate. The following is known.

1F pitches before C.2The Agri startup pitches immediately after the Edtech startup.3The Health startup pitches immediately after the Logistics startup.4B and D pitch in consecutive slots.5The Edtech startup pitches immediately after the Climate startup.6A is the Edtech startup, B is the Fintech startup, C is the Logistics startup, D is the Climate startup and E is the Health startup.

The investor has a fixed budget. She hears the pitches in slot order and funds each one in full, in order, until she reaches a startup whose ask she cannot fully meet. She then stops. The asks, in ₹ crore, are below.

items.detail: Ask

items.title: B
items.detail: Ask

items.title: C
items.detail: Ask

items.title: D
items.detail: Ask

items.title: E
items.detail: Ask

items.detail: Ask

blocks.html: Q1. Which startup pitches in slot 4? (a) A (b) C (c) E (d) F
Q2. What is the total ask, in ₹ crore, of the startups that pitch before the Edtech startup? (a) 7 (b) 8 (c) 10 (d) 13
Q3. Her budget is ₹15 cr. Which startup is the first she cannot fully fund, and how much of her budget is left? (a) F, ₹2 cr (b) F, ₹5 cr (c) C, ₹2 cr (d) C, ₹7 cr
Q4. Suppose condition 4 (B and D are consecutive) is removed and everything else stays. How many different pitch orders are possible? (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4
Q5. Using the original conditions, her budget is ₹20 cr. How many startups does she fund in full? (a) 3 (b) 4 (c) 5 (d) 6

blocks.title: Answers and worked solutions
blocks.kicker: Don't scroll on until you've tried

blocks.html: Setup. Sectors are fixed for five startups, so F is Agri. Condition 5 and 2 chain the sectors: Climate, then Edtech, then Agri, in consecutive slots, which means D, A, F in that order. Condition 3 gives C then E in consecutive slots. Condition 4 says B is next to D. D has A right after it, so B must be right before D. That block is B, D, A, F. Condition 1 puts C after F, so C and E follow. The only order is B (Fintech), D (Climate), A (Edtech), F (Agri), C (Logistics), E (Health). I checked this by exhaustive search: it is the only arrangement that meets every condition.
Q1: (d) F. Slot 4 is F.
Q2: (c) 10. Edtech is A in slot 3. B and D pitch before it, so 4 + 6 = 10.
Q3: (a) F, ₹2 cr. In order: B takes 4, D takes 6 (total 10), A takes 3 (total 13). F asks 5 but only 2 remains, so she stops at F with ₹2 cr left.
Q4: (c) 3. Without condition 4, D, A, F stay together and C, E stay together with F before C. The orders possible are B D A F C E, D A F B C E and D A F C E B. That is three.
Q5: (b) 4. B 4, D 6, A 3, F 5 add up to 18. C asks 7, which would take the total to 25, so she funds four and stops at C with ₹2 cr left.
